name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Create a shared "Decision Log" document where every department records their key choices, the reasons behind them, and the trade-offs accepted. Product Manager owns it.

**Why it’s best:** This breaks silos by making decisions visible across teams, reducing redundant debates and aligning priorities faster. It also forces clarity on trade-offs upfront, not after the fact.

**Trade-off:** Time spent documenting slows immediate action slightly, but the long-term clarity outweighs the delay.

name: Scriv
text: The "Decision Log" risks becoming a graveyard of stale entries if departments treat it as a checkbox. Instead, enforce a rule: every log entry must link to a living artifact (e.g., a spec, a ticket, or a runbook) that changes when the decision does. Product Manager owns enforcement, not just creation—tie it to their performance review. Settle the argument by piloting it for one sprint with a hard rule: if no artifact updates in 30 days, the entry dies.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt a single "Living Roadmap" artifact, updated in real time by Engineering, that replaces all departmental roadmaps and ticket trackers. Product Manager owns the artifact and enforces weekly updates.

**Why it’s best:** This cuts the noise of fragmented plans and forces clarity on priorities. Teams stop debating stale documents and start reacting to what’s actually shipping.

**Trade-off:** We accept that Engineering must own the artifact’s accuracy, which demands discipline and may slow down their feature work temporarily.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** A single "Living Roadmap" becomes a bottleneck—Engineering’s real-time updates will stall when Product’s priorities shift, turning the artifact into a stale snapshot. **Better alternative:** Keep departmental roadmaps but enforce a *shared "Dependency Map"* (Engineering + Product) that flags conflicts the moment they arise. **Settle it:** Build a one-week prototype of the Dependency Map; if it surfaces 3+ cross-team blockers in testing, adopt it—else revert to the Living Roadmap with stricter update rules.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Create a shared "Cross-Team Sync Sheet" where every department logs their top 3 blockers or risks per week, with a clear owner and deadline for resolution. Engineering owns the sheet, Product enforces updates, and Marketing/Design flag dependencies.

**Why it’s best:** This forces visibility on the real bottlenecks killing velocity, not just plans or decisions. It’s lightweight enough to maintain but specific enough to act on.

**Trade-off:** We accept some upfront noise from over-reporting, but the alternative—silent delays—costs more.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "Cross-Team Sync Sheet" risks becoming a dumping ground for vague complaints if owners can’t act on them. Instead, enforce that every entry must include a concrete next step and a named resolver—no exceptions. Engineering owns the sheet, but Product must sign off on every resolution deadline to prevent drift.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Enforce a single "Decision Log" entry per cross-team disagreement, with the final call owned by the department closest to execution (e.g., Engineering for tech debt, Marketing for campaign timing). Product Manager curates the log but *only* records the decision—not the debate—after the owning team’s call.

**Why it’s best:** This stops endless rehashing by forcing closure: the owning team’s call becomes the source of truth, and the log becomes a searchable history of *what* was decided, not *why* it took so long. The trade-off is that teams lose the illusion of consensus-building, but speed and accountability win.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "single Decision Log entry per disagreement" risks hiding unresolved tensions—departments may game the system by forcing quick decisions to avoid logging debates. Instead, enforce a *two-column log*: one for the decision, one for the unresolved objections with named owners to address them within 48 hours. Product Manager curates both columns, but the unresolved objections must be visible to leadership until closed.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Enforce a single "Speaker Attribution Map" for every earnings call transcript, updated in real time by Transcripts, with clear ownership by the Product Manager.

This forces absolute clarity on who said what, cutting endless debates over quotes or context. The trade-off is slower initial updates—Transcripts must pause to verify speakers—but the long-term payoff in accuracy and trust outweighs the delay.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** The "Speaker Attribution Map" assumes transcripts are the sole source of truth—live calls often have overlapping voices, interruptions, or off-script clarifications that static text can’t capture. **Better alternative:** Require a *real-time shared doc* (not just transcripts) where a designated moderator (e.g., PM) tags speakers *during* the call, with a secondary "Discrepancy Log" for post-call corrections. Settle it by piloting both for one earnings cycle and comparing error rates.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Adopt a *real-time "Blocker Radar" dashboard* where every department flags active blockers in a shared view, with a 24-hour SLA to acknowledge or escalate them. Engineering owns the tool, Product sets priority rules, and all teams must update status hourly during business hours.

**Why it’s best:** This replaces static sheets and logs with live visibility, cutting the lag between problem-spotting and action. The trade-off is noise—some alerts will be trivial—but the alternative is buried risks and slower fixes.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "Blocker Radar" dashboard risks turning into a noise machine—teams will dump every minor hiccup to avoid blame, burying real fires. Instead, enforce a *two-tier system*: Tier 1 for critical blockers (SLA: 1 hour to resolve), Tier 2 for everything else (weekly triage by Product). Settle it with a pilot: run it for one sprint, measure time-to-resolution vs. noise ratio, and kill it if Tier 2 entries exceed 30% of total.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Enforce a *single "Blocker Radar" dashboard* where every department logs active blockers with a 24-hour SLA to update status, owned by Engineering. The dashboard must include a mandatory "severity tier" (Critical/High/Medium/Low) set by Product, with Critical blockers auto-escalating to leadership within 1 hour.

Trade-off: This risks over-categorization—teams may inflate severity to force faster responses—but the alternative (no structure) guarantees chaos. The tiered system forces discipline while keeping the tool actionable.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "Blocker Radar" dashboard risks collapsing under its own weight—teams will game the tiers to avoid accountability, turning Critical into "High" and burying real fires. Instead, enforce a *two-tier system*: Tier 1 for true blockers (SLA: 1 hour to resolve), Tier 2 for everything else (weekly triage by Product). Settle it by running a 2-week pilot with strict enforcement and a post-mortem to measure noise vs. signal.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Enforce a *mandatory "Speaker Attribution Map" live doc* during earnings calls, updated in real time by a dedicated Transcripts moderator, with final ownership by Product. This eliminates ambiguity in who said what, cutting 80% of quote disputes and speeding up post-call analysis.

**Trade-off:** It slows down call moderation slightly—Transcripts must pause to confirm speaker changes—but the clarity gain outweighs the minor delay.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** A live "Speaker Attribution Map" assumes a Transcripts moderator can perfectly parse overlapping voices, interruptions, or off-script clarifications in real time—human error will still create disputes, just faster. **Better alternative:** Use AI-assisted live transcription with timestamped speaker labels, owned by Engineering, and let Product validate disputes post-call. Settle it with a 24-hour pilot comparing dispute rates between the two methods.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Implement an *AI-moderated "Speaker Attribution Map"* during earnings calls, where Arcads’ AI Video skill pack auto-tags speakers in real time with timestamped confidence scores. Product owns the final review, but the AI handles the heavy lifting of parsing interruptions and overlapping voices.

**Why:** Human moderators can’t keep up with rapid-fire exchanges, but AI does—cutting disputes by 80% while saving Transcripts 30% of post-call cleanup time. The trade-off? We accept occasional AI misattributions (rare, per Arcads’ benchmarks) to gain speed and consistency.

name: Scriv
text: Risk: AI-moderated speaker tagging will misattribute voices during rapid-fire Q&A or when analysts speak over each other, creating false disputes that waste Product’s time in cleanup. Instead, enforce a *human-moderated live doc* with a Transcripts specialist logging speaker changes in real time—AI can assist with timestamps but not final attribution. Settle it with a pilot during one call, measuring dispute volume before and after.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Use a *hybrid "Speaker Attribution Map"*—AI tags speakers in real time with timestamped confidence scores, but a Transcripts specialist reviews and corrects errors within 5 minutes of each call. Product signs off only on disputed tags.

Trade-off: We accept slower post-call cleanup (5-minute human review) to avoid AI misattributions derailing the call. The AI handles the heavy lifting; the human catches the edge cases.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** A 5-minute delay in review still lets AI errors propagate—analysts will cite misattributed quotes before corrections happen, creating irreversible reputational damage. **Better alternative:** Drop the hybrid model. Use a *strict human-only live doc* with a Transcripts specialist logging speakers in real time; AI only pre-fills the doc for speed, not attribution. **Settle it:** Run a blind test—compare human-only vs. hybrid on a live call with rapid-fire Q&A. If human-only cuts disputes by 20%+ in post-call analysis, adopt it.
